2.3.7.1-f104.accuracy_reason: The maxim is in the Formula vitae honestae (Martin of Braga), which circulated under Seneca's name; the note hedges this properly.

2.3.7.1-f105.accuracy_reason: The Latin renders the Delphic/Seven Sages maxim ἐγγύα, πάρα δ' ἄτα (often credited to Thales).

2.3.7.1-f107.accuracy_reason: Persius 4.52 has 'tecum habita: noris quam sit tibi curta supellex', and the note gives the sense correctly.

2.3.7.1-f109.accuracy_reason: Occasion was pictured with a forelock in front and bald behind (the line is from the Disticha Catonis 2.26: 'fronte capillata, post est occasio calva').

2.3.7.1-f112.accuracy_reason: The lines are Horace, Epistles 1.18.37–38, and the next line Burton quotes is 1.18.39, so 'ep. 19' is indeed wrong. The standard text reads 'illius' and goes on 'et vino tortus et ira'.

2.3.7.1-f114.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.7 reads 'nec te quaesiveris extra', and the note gives its sense correctly.

2.3.7.1-f116.accuracy_reason: Solon's law against neutrality in civil strife is reported by Aristotle (Ath. Pol. 8.5) and discussed in Gellius 2.12.

2.3.7.1-f118.accuracy_reason: Anteros appears in Phaedrus 255d. Anteros as a brother of Eros and son of Venus comes from later sources such as Cicero and Themistius.

2.3.7.1-f121.accuracy_reason: Erasmus does collect the proverb (Adagia 1.2.29, from πρὸς Κρῆτα κρητίζειν), but I cannot confirm that his Latin heading is either form the note gives.

2.3.7.1-f128.accuracy_reason: The usual form of this Publilius Syrus sententia, as I recall it, is 'veterem ferendo iniuriam invitas novam', not 'invites'; the note does not name the source.

2.3.7.1-f140.accuracy_reason: Adelphoe 415–416 (Demea on looking into other men's lives as into a mirror) fits the precept, and the note rightly hedges with 'probably'.

2.3.7.1-f141.accuracy_reason: The pun on salarium and sal (salt, also wit) is right, and 'multis' is the plausible correction.

2.3.7.1-f15.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.54–55 reads 'magna petis, Phaethon, et quae nec viribus istis / munera conveniant nec tam puerilibus annis'.

2.3.7.1-f158.accuracy_reason: Cato lost the praetorian election for 55 BC to Vatinius, which was the classic example of an unworthy man preferred to a worthy one.

2.3.7.1-f161.accuracy_reason: This is the opening of Ausonius's epigram on Agathocles ('Fortunam reverenter habe, quicumque repente / dives ab exili progrediere loco'), and the note gives its warning correctly.

2.3.7.1-f18.accuracy_reason: The line is from Ovid, Fasti 1.419 ('fastus inest pulchris, sequiturque superbia formam'), where forma means beauty. The note names no work, so it does not repeat the mistake in Burton's sidenote ('Met.').

2.3.7.1-f20.accuracy_reason: Diogenes Laertius 2.37 tells how Socrates refused to hit Xanthippe back so that onlookers would not cheer them on; eia is a cry of encouragement.

2.3.7.1-f22.accuracy_reason: It is a proverbial jingle, and the explanation of the image is correct.

2.3.7.1-f27.accuracy_reason: The text is Terence, Adelphoe 860–861, 're ipsa repperi / facilitate nihil esse homini melius neque clementia'; Burton reorders the words and drops 'neque'.

2.3.7.1-f29.accuracy_reason: The reference to Ovid, Tristia 3.5.31–32 is correct, and in that context 'faciles motus' means being readily moved to relent.

2.3.7.1-f32.accuracy_reason: In Aeneid 4.449 the words describe Aeneas standing firm against the pleas Anna brings him from Dido.

2.3.7.1-f34.accuracy_reason: In the prologue to Plautus's Rudens, Arcturus says that Jupiter re-judges cases won by perjury and fines the winners more heavily; the second line is translated correctly.

2.3.7.1-f40.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate wording is quoted correctly ('per quae peccat quis, per haec et torquetur'). It is Wisdom 11:17 in the Clementine Vulgate but 11:16 in English Bibles and in Burton's sidenote, which is a small numbering difference.

2.3.7.1-f41.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.112–113 reads 'sine caede ac vulnere'; the notes on Pluto as Ceres' son-in-law and on 'dry death' are correct.

2.3.7.1-f47.accuracy_reason: The Septuagint of Genesis 4:7 ('hēmartes; hēsychason') became 'peccasti, quiesce' in the Old Latin, and Ambrose quotes it in that form.

2.3.7.1-f5.accuracy_reason: The source is right: Horace, Satires 2.5.10, where Tiresias advises Ulysses on legacy-hunting. But the claim that the sidenote stands in the preceding paragraph can't be checked, because the item gives no sidenotes and the preceding text isn't shown.

2.3.7.1-f50.accuracy_reason: This is a proverb collected by Erasmus ('habet et musca splenem'; 'inest et formicae bilis'), and Burton's English does turn the ant into a bee with a sting.

2.3.7.1-f55.accuracy_reason: Velleius 2.35 does say this of Cato Uticensis ('numquam recte fecit ut facere videretur, sed quia aliter facere non potuerat'), and Burton applies it to Censorius.

2.3.7.1-f56.accuracy_reason: Ammianus 18.1.4 gives Julian's retort as 'ecquis innocens esse poterit, si accusasse sufficiet?', and 'clam vel palam' is not in it.

2.3.7.1-f58.accuracy_reason: The fragment does come from the proverbial line 'felix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum'.

2.3.7.1-f59.accuracy_reason: It is a medieval rhyming proverb, the certo/certo pun is real, and 'sterco' is a non-classical form.

2.3.7.1-f64.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of 2 Corinthians 6:8 reads 'per infamiam et bonam famam'.

2.3.7.1-f80.accuracy_reason: Catullus 64.338 reads 'nascetur vobis expers terroris Achilles', and 'armatus' is not in it.

2.3.7.1-f84.accuracy_reason: Seneca's De constantia sapientis is about exactly this theme (the wise man is untouched by insult), and Burton names Seneca but no work.

2.3.7.1-f86.accuracy_reason: The line is Persius 1.58. The stork gesture is correctly explained, and Janus, with his face behind, cannot be mocked from behind.

2.3.7.1-f89.accuracy_reason: The saying is attributed to Antisthenes (in Diogenes Laertius and Marcus Aurelius) and to Alexander (in Plutarch).

2.3.7.1-f9.accuracy_reason: Dio 47.49 reports that Brutus quoted these tragic verses in Greek before his death.

2.3.7.1-f92.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Cons. 1 pr. 4 does continue 'quotiens ostentando quis factum recipit famae pretium'. The first sentence appears to be Burton's own framing.
